slides.title: Order saved, but the news got lost
slides.tldr: Writing to the database and sending a message are two separate systems, so one transaction can't cover both; a crash in between does one and not the other (a dual write).

blocks.body: Ryan's order service saves order 101 to the database, then is supposed to send an `OrderPlaced` message to the message broker (the post office that carries messages between services) so the stock service can set the goods aside. Right between the commit and the publish, the server crashes. The order exists, but nobody heard about it: stock is never reserved, and the customer never gets the product. This is called a **dual write**: one fact written to two places, with no way to tie the two writes together.

blocks.caption: The commit succeeded, but the server crashed before publishing

actors.label: Order service
actors.tip: Responsible for both saving the order and sending the event, but these happen in two different systems.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Has its own transaction, but knows nothing about the broker.

actors.label: Message broker
actors.tip: Tells the stock service when it receives an event. If nothing arrives, it tells nobody anything.

messages.tip: The database part is done but the broker part is not. This gap is always there.
Stock will never be reserved, because nobody even knows about the order.

blocks.body: Writing to the database and sending a message never happen in one transaction: there is always a gap in between.

items: Reversing the order (publish first, commit after) is no better: if the commit fails, an event goes out for an order that doesn't exist.
A `try/catch` doesn't close this gap, because when the process crashes, the catch block doesn't run either.

items.meaning: Writing the same fact to two separate systems that have no atomic transaction between them.
A group of database changes that either all succeed together or all roll back.

check.q: What problem do you get if you publish first and commit afterwards?
check.a: If the commit fails, the event has already gone out but the order doesn't exist. The stock service will reserve goods for an order that never existed.

slides.title: The "to be sent" ledger: transactional outbox
slides.tldr: Write the event to an outbox table in your own database, in the same transaction as the data; a separate relay sends it to the broker later, so the fact and the news can never drift apart.

blocks.title: The store's "to be sent" ledger
blocks.body: A store owner writes "10 pounds of rice for Rachel" in the sales ledger, and **on the same page, with the same pen**, writes "tell the warehouse". Both are written together, so you never get one without the other. Later the delivery driver goes round and carries those "tell the warehouse" lines to the warehouse, ticking each one off when it's delivered. If he stops halfway, the line is still there and someone else will send it.

blocks.caption: The order and the event share one transaction; sending is the relay's job

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.tip: Writes the order and the event in the same transaction. Never calls the broker directly.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Both tables are written in one transaction, so either both rows exist or neither does.

nodes.label: Relay
nodes.tip: A separate process that finds unsent rows in the outbox and delivers them to the broker.

nodes.label: Message broker
nodes.tip: Accepts the event and hands it to the consumers.

edges.label: The order and the outbox row are written in one transaction
The relay looks for unsent rows in the outbox
The relay publishes the rows to the broker
It stamps sent_at on the delivered rows

blocks.body: If the relay crashes after publishing but before it sets `sent_at`, that event goes out again. So an outbox gives you **at-least-once** delivery: an event is never lost, but it may arrive twice. That double delivery is why the consumer needs an **inbox**. The price: events leave a second or so later, and you must run the relay and clean the table.

items.meaning: A table in your own database where events meant for the outside world are written first.
The process that reads the outbox and sends the events out.

aside.body: Write in the ledger first, the delivery driver sends later. The fact and the news share one pen.

check.q: Which problem goes away when the event and the order are written in the same transaction?
check.a: The mismatch where the order exists but the event doesn't (or the reverse). The two either commit together or roll back together.

slides.title: Writing the outbox and running the relay: Doctrine and Messenger
slides.tldr: Persist the Order and an OutboxMessage in one flush; the relay picks a batch with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, dispatches it on the Messenger bus and sets sent_at.

marks.tip: The whole block is one transaction. If an exception is thrown, the order and the outbox row both roll back.
The message id is created right here. The consumer will later use this id to spot duplicates.
The event does not go to the broker directly: it just becomes a row in the outbox table.
SKIP LOCKED: when several relays run at once, each skips the rows another has taken, so the work is shared without blocking.
The actual publish. If it throws, the transaction rolls back: this row and any rows of the batch already sent stay unsent and go out again. The inbox absorbs that.
The dispatch succeeded, but if we crash before this write, the event goes out again. That is the price of at-least-once.

items: Run the relay from a console command or a Scheduler task, every second or every few seconds. Delete old sent rows after about a week.
A lighter option: if Messenger's Doctrine transport uses the same connection, `dispatch()` itself behaves like an outbox. You need the relay above only when publishing to a separate broker.

items.desc: your own command: loops over publishBatch() every second or so

check.q: Why does the relay use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`?
check.a: When two relays run at once, they split the rows instead of both taking the same one. A row locked by one relay is skipped by the other, which moves on to the next.

slides.title: The two tables: outbox and inbox
slides.tldr: The outbox needs an index on unsent rows and a cleanup job; the inbox needs a unique key on (message_id, handler) and a retention period longer than any late duplicate.

blocks.body: Both patterns stand on two small tables. With no index on the unsent rows, the relay walks every old row on every poll: at 100,000 events a day that is 36 million rows after a year, when it wants the 50 not yet sent. With no cleanup, both tables grow forever. Create them in a Doctrine Migration.

marks.tip: The index holds only unsent rows, so it stays tiny however many old rows pile up. The relay reads it instead of the whole table.
Run it daily from a Scheduler task. Once a row is sent it is only history.
This key is what `ON CONFLICT (message_id, handler)` relies on. Without it the insert never conflicts and every duplicate gets through.
Keep rows longer than the longest time a duplicate can still arrive. Delete too early and a late duplicate looks new.

items: MySQL has no partial index: index `(sent_at, created_at)` instead, and use `INSERT IGNORE` in place of `ON CONFLICT`.
Set the inbox retention from your broker's longest redelivery window, not from guesswork.

check.q: A year in, the relay is slow although only 50 rows are unsent. What do you look at first?
check.a: The index. With none on the unsent rows, every poll walks millions of old rows. A partial index on `sent_at IS NULL` reads just the 50.

slides.title: Arrives twice, runs once: dedup with an inbox
slides.tldr: An outbox is at-least-once, so the consumer will see the same message twice; the handler inserts the message id into an inbox table in the same transaction to skip duplicates.

blocks.body: If the relay crashes and sends the same `OrderPlaced` twice, a naive handler reduces stock twice. The fix: the receiver keeps a **delivery register** (the inbox). The first time a message id arrives, it writes the id in the register and does the work. The second time, it sees "this delivery was already taken in" and walks away.

marks.tip: The handler has no idea whether it has seen this message before. With at-least-once delivery, that is a bug.
A unique constraint on (message_id, handler). The same message cannot get a second row for this handler.
0 rows means it was already handled. Just return; throwing an exception would make Messenger retry for nothing.
The inbox write and the stock change share one transaction, so if the work fails, the inbox row rolls back too.

blocks.body: The outbox guarantees the sending side, the inbox guarantees the receiving side. Together they give you "effectively once".

items.meaning: Safe to run twice: the second run changes nothing.
A database rule that refuses a second row with the same key.

aside.body: Outbox = never lost. Inbox = never run twice.

use: Saving to the database and publishing an event are both essential, together
Running the consumer's work twice would do harm (stock, money, email)
avoid: The work is naturally idempotent (like "set the status"), where a separate inbox may not be needed

check.q: What goes wrong if the inbox insert and the real work are in separate transactions?
check.a: If you crash after the insert but before the work, the message counts as "done" although nothing happened. The retry sees the earlier row and returns, so the work never gets done.

slides.title: Money taken, stock held, no courier
slides.tldr: Work spread over several services can't sit in one database transaction; if a middle step fails, the earlier steps stay done and the order hangs half-finished.

blocks.body: Ryan's order flow is split across three services: payment, stock and courier. Rachel places an order, the payment service takes her money, the stock service sets the goods aside, and then the courier service says "no couriers available today". Each of the three services has its own database, so a single `ROLLBACK` can't undo everything. Rachel's money is gone, the goods are held, and the order goes nowhere.

blocks.caption: The third step fails, and the first two stay done

actors.label: Order service
actors.tip: Its job is to run the whole order, step by step.

actors.label: Payment
actors.tip: Has already charged the money and committed in its own database.

actors.label: Stock
actors.tip: Has already held the goods and committed in its own database.

actors.label: Courier
actors.tip: No courier is free today, so it reports failure.

messages.note: Money taken, goods held, order hanging
messages.tip: Two steps were committed earlier. They won't undo themselves now.

blocks.body: Work across many services will break midway. Decide in advance how the earlier steps get undone.

aside.body: Every service has its own database, so running one transaction over all of them is hard and slow (two-phase commit). A saga replaces it with a chain of small transactions plus a defined way back.

check.q: Why can't a single `ROLLBACK` undo everything here?
check.a: The payment and stock services have already committed in their own separate databases. Committed work can't be rolled back.

slides.title: Canceling the wedding bookings: compensating actions
slides.tldr: A saga is a chain of small local transactions, each with an undo action (a compensation); when one fails, the earlier steps are canceled in reverse order.

blocks.title: Canceling the wedding bookings
blocks.body: For a wedding you've booked a community hall, a caterer and a photographer, and each took a deposit. Then the photographer says he can't come. You can't just "erase" the other bookings, because the deposits are already paid. Instead you do **new work**: call the caterer to cancel, ask for the deposit back, tell the hall. You may not get all of it back.

blocks.caption: Steps move forward; when the courier fails, the undo actions run

nodes.label: Charge money
nodes.tip: The payment service charges the money in its own transaction and commits.

nodes.label: Hold goods
nodes.tip: The stock service holds the goods in its own transaction and commits.

nodes.label: Book courier
nodes.tip: This step fails. From here on, the undo actions of the earlier steps must run.

nodes.label: Release goods
nodes.tip: The stock compensation: put the held goods back on sale.

nodes.label: Refund money
nodes.tip: The payment compensation: return the charged money to the customer.

edges.label: Money is charged, now hold the goods
Goods are held, now book the courier
The courier failed, so release the stock first

blocks.body: This is called a **semantic rollback**. It isn't a real rollback (nothing is erased); it's a new action that undoes the earlier one in meaning. So the books still show that the money was charged and later refunded.

items.meaning: A chain of small local transactions where each step has an undo action.
A new action that reverses the effect of an earlier one in meaning, rather than erasing it.

aside.body: Undoing is not erasing. Undoing is a new action in the opposite direction.

check.q: Why do compensations run in reverse order, and why isn't this a "real rollback"?
check.a: A later step may depend on an earlier one, so the later one is undone first. And nothing is erased: a new action is added, and the history stays in the books.

slides.title: Saga state in the database: building an orchestrator
slides.tldr: Store the saga's step in an OrderSaga entity; an orchestrator, as Messenger handlers, listens to events and either sends the next command or runs compensations on failure.

blocks.body: An orchestrator that lives only in memory forgets everything on a server restart. So the saga's position is written to a table: the step, a deadline and the reason for any failure. Whenever an event arrives, the orchestrator reads the table, changes the step and sends the next command.

marks.tip: Which step the saga is on now. This is what lets work continue after a restart or crash.
If the step doesn't advance by this time, the sweeper treats the saga as timed out (next slide).
If the saga isn't at the expected step, the event is old or a duplicate. Do nothing and return.
The flush and the dispatch are separate steps with a gap between them. Close it with an outbox.
Compensation runs in reverse: the refund happens only after the news that stock was released.

items: Put the saga/order id in every command, and make every handler idempotent. Duplicate events will happen.
Use an [[workflows/outbox-inbox/save-then-crash|outbox]] to close the gap around the dispatch.

items.label: Organizing steps with a state machine

check.q: What happens if the orchestrator keeps the saga step in memory instead of the database?
check.a: On a restart or crash it forgets which order was at which step, so half-finished orders hang and nobody can run their undo actions.

slides.title: Conductor or dance troupe: orchestration vs choreography
slides.tldr: In orchestration one conductor decides the steps; in choreography each service listens for events and triggers the next one itself. With many or complex steps, orchestration is easier.

blocks.title: A wedding planner versus everyone for themselves
blocks.body: Orchestration is the wedding planner who tells everyone who does what and when, and who knows exactly where things got stuck. Choreography has no manager: the cook finishes and calls the waiter, the waiter serves and tells the decorator. Nobody sees the whole picture.

blocks.caption: The two kinds of saga side by side

rows.tip: In orchestration the whole story is written in one place. In choreography it is spread across the events.

cells: Piece it together from all services
rows.tip: To find a bug, you look at the orchestrator's table and see the step.
In choreography services don't know each other directly, so the coupling is loose.
Adding a step looks easy in choreography, but who depends on whom gets lost.

cells: Small flows of two or three steps
rows.tip: As steps grow, the web of events in choreography becomes hard to follow.

blocks.body: Choreography for simple flows of two or three steps; orchestration when there are many steps or conditions.

items: Don't let the orchestrator swell with business rules. It should handle only order and failures; the rules belong in the services.
Cycles (A→B→A) are easy to create in choreography, and nobody notices.

check.q: For a flow with ten steps, a few conditions and timeouts, which would you pick, and why?
check.a: Orchestration. The whole sequence, the conditions and the timeouts can be read in one place, so bugs are easier to find and changes easier to make. In choreography that complexity gets lost in the web of events.

slides.title: Stuck sagas and failing compensations
slides.tldr: A deadline lets a sweeper catch silence, but a timeout only means "no answer yet"; compensations must be idempotent and retried forever, and steps that can't be undone go last.

blocks.body: The hardest thing to handle is silence: the courier service simply never answers. The saga would hang forever. So every saga gets a **deadline**, and a sweeper treats sagas past their deadline as timed out and starts compensation. One warning: silence is not the same as failure. The next slide shows why.

marks.tip: Sagas stuck at a step that isn't finished, and whose time has run out.
A timeout is an event the orchestrator can react to. It is not a plain failure: the step may have worked (next slide).

blocks.title: Rules for compensations
items: Make compensations idempotent: even if `refund` runs twice, the money goes back only once (use a key).
If a compensation fails, keep retrying. "The undo failed" is never a place to stop.
Put steps that can't be undone (sending an email, a courier leaving) at the very end.
Alert a human for anything that can't be undone.

blocks.body: A compensation never gives up with "failed". It retries until it succeeds, so it must be idempotent.

items: A step that can't be undone is called a pivot step. Keep every step before it undoable, and every step after it guaranteed to succeed (retryable).
Give the compensation its own idempotency key: `saga-refund-<orderId>`.

check.q: If the refund compensation fails with a network error, what should the saga do, and why?
check.a: Try again with the same idempotency key. If it stopped, the customer's money would stay taken, and the key guarantees that a retry won't refund twice.

slides.title: A timeout is not a failure: the step may have worked
slides.tldr: A timed-out step has an unknown outcome: cancel it too, by its own key, before undoing the earlier steps, and refuse its late reply.

blocks.body: The saga is at `reserved`, waiting for the courier. Five minutes pass and the sweeper fires. But the courier service isn't dead, only slow: at minute six it books van #88, and its reply gets lost. If the saga now undoes only the stock and the payment, Rachel gets her money back, and a courier turns up for an order that no longer exists. A timeout means "no answer yet", not "it failed". The step's outcome is **unknown**, so undo it as if it had worked.

blocks.caption: The same timeout, handled two ways

columns.title: Timeout = plain failure
items: Undo only stock and payment
The courier step is treated as "never happened"
Minute 6: van #88 is booked and nobody cancels it
A courier arrives for a dead order
columns.tip: The saga assumes the courier step never ran, so nothing undoes it.

columns.title: Timeout = outcome unknown
items: Cancel the courier step too, by its own key
Cancel works whether the booking exists or not
A late "book" request hits the canceled key and is refused
Then release stock, then refund, as before
columns.tip: The saga cancels the courier step by its key, which is safe whether or not it ran.

marks.tip: The sweeper may fire again before this handler finishes. Only a saga still in progress is compensated.
The step in flight gets its own cancel, with the same key that booked it.
The cancel may arrive before the booking it cancels. The marker closes that race.
Canceling twice is harmless, so the saga can retry this as often as it needs.

items: The same goes for any step in flight: after a timeout at `started`, the payment may have gone through, so cancel it by its key too.
Price: one extra message and one marker row per timed-out step. Skip it for steps that only read data, since there is nothing to cancel.

check.q: The saga timed out waiting for the courier. Why must it cancel the courier step too, not just stock and payment?
check.a: A timeout means no answer, not no booking. The courier may have booked a van and lost its reply. Canceling by key is safe either way, and the marker refuses a late booking.

slides.title: I changed the number, and now the books don't add up
slides.tldr: Overwriting the original payment amount for a partial refund destroys history; at month end the gateway's books and ours disagree and nobody can say why.

blocks.body: Rachel returns a $30 item from a $120 order. Ryan's support agent takes the easy way out: he edits `payment.amount` from $120 to $90. At month end the accountant sits down to match the gateway's statement against the database and finds that the gateway says $120 collected while the database says $90. $30 went back, but when, why and who did it is written nowhere.

blocks.caption: Overwriting the amount destroys the original fact

actors.label: Support agent
actors.tip: Handles the refund request. Takes what looks like the simple route and edits the amount directly.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Treats whatever was last written as the truth. Keeps no way to get the earlier value back.

actors.label: Accountant
actors.tip: At month end, matches the gateway's statement against our books.

messages.tip: Now there is no way to say how much was actually collected, or how much went back.

blocks.body: A money record never changes. What happened becomes a new record, linked to the old one.

aside.body: Change the original record and you lose the answer to "what happened?". Audits, dispute handling and reconciliation with the gateway all rest on history.

check.q: Exactly which facts are lost when the amount goes from $120 to $90?
check.a: That $120 was originally collected, that $30 went back, and when, why and by whom. Only one number is left, and it explains none of this.

slides.title: The return slip: don't tear the original, write a new one
slides.tldr: The original payment stays untouched; each refund is a new Refund record linked to it, and the remaining refundable amount is calculated.

blocks.title: The store receipt and return slip
blocks.body: Once a store receipt is printed, nobody tears it up or scribbles on it. When goods come back, the clerk writes a new return slip saying "$30 returned against original receipt number 552". Put the two side by side and the whole history is clear. The remaining amount isn't kept in anyone's head; it comes from adding and subtracting the two slips.

blocks.caption: Two refunds against one payment, the original unchanged

rows.tip: The original collection. This record never changes again.
The first refund. Linked to P-1, with its own reason and timestamp.
The second partial refund, as a separate record.
$120 − $30 − $20 = $70. This value isn't stored; it is worked out each time.

blocks.title: Why this shape works
items: The whole history is kept: who, when, why, how much.
Reconciling with the gateway is easy: every Refund matches one gateway refund.
Several partial refunds on the same payment are handled naturally.

items.meaning: Canceling an authorization before the money has moved. The money is still with the customer.
Returning money to the customer in a new transaction, after it has been collected.
The customer's bank raises a dispute and forces the money back.

check.q: Why is the remaining refundable amount calculated each time instead of stored in a payment column?
check.a: A separately updated column can drift out of step with the refunds, and you lose track of who changed it and when. When you add and subtract, the records are the only source of truth.

slides.title: Creating a Refund record: limits, locks and idempotency
slides.tldr: Lock the Payment with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE, count the remaining refundable amount, persist a new Refund; if the same idempotency key arrives again, return the earlier one.

marks.tip: The original amount is changed, and if two people refund at once, more than the limit can go back.
Locks the payment row. Another refund on the same payment waits until this transaction ends.
If the client retries, the earlier Refund with the same key is returned; no second payout.
Remaining = original − sum of all earlier refunds. Calculated inside the lock, so the number is true right now.
The gateway call happens outside the transaction, via the outbox. Handling an unknown result from that call is a separate topic.

items: Always store money as integers (minor units), never floats. Keep a Refund amount positive; the type (Refund) already says it goes back.
Add a unique constraint on `(payment_id, idem_key)` so the database stops a duplicate even if the lock is missed.

items.meaning: While one transaction holds a payment's lock, others who want it wait in line, like one person in a phone booth.
A unique tag sent with a request, so the server can tell a retry from a new request.
A table where "call the gateway" is written in the same transaction; a worker sends it afterwards.

check.q: Two support agents each refund $80 on a $120 payment at the same moment, with no lock. What can happen?
check.a: Both see $120 remaining, so both $80 refunds pass and $160 goes back. With a lock, the second sees $40 remaining and rejects the $80.

slides.title: Partial capture and partial shipments
slides.tldr: An authorization holds the money once; each shipment captures exactly its share as a separate record, and any share that will never ship is voided (a reversal).

blocks.body: In online shopping the money is first **held** (authorized) and only **taken** (captured) when the goods ship. Rachel has 3 items at $40 each, so $120 is held. Two ship first, so $80 is captured. If the third is delayed, the remaining $40 is captured with a later shipment, or released (voided). Each one is a new record.

blocks.caption: One authorization, a few captures and a void

rows.tip: $120 is held on the customer's card, but the money hasn't been taken yet.
Two items shipped, so $80 was taken. A-1 hasn't changed; the new record is C-1.
When the third item ships, the remaining $40 is taken. Nothing is held any more.
This happens instead of C-2: the remaining $40 is released. The money never moved, so this is a reversal, not a refund.

blocks.title: Rules
items: The sum of all captures and voids never exceeds the authorization.
Each capture is linked to a shipment, so you know which money was for which goods.
Returning money after a capture is a refund, not a void.

aside.body: Releasing held money is a void. Returning taken money is a refund.

items: An authorization usually expires within a few days. A late shipment may need a new authorization, so check your gateway's rules.

check.q: Rachel cancels the third item. What record covers the remaining $40: a refund or a void? Why?
check.a: A void. That $40 was never taken, only held. A refund applies only once the money has been collected.

slides.title: Don't hard-code the fee: compute it from rules
slides.tldr: A hard-coded refund fee needs a deploy for every rule change and drifts on floats; keep the rules in a table staff can edit, calculate in integers, and record the fee separately.

blocks.body: "Returns after 7 days lose 10%." A rule like this changes a few times a year. Write `if ($days > 7) $fee = $amount * 0.1;` in code and every change is a code change plus a deploy, while floats make the cents drift. Keep the rules in a database table instead, and calculate in integers (basis points, where 10% = 1000). Putting them in `services.yaml` is only half a fix: that file ships with the code, so changing it still means a deploy.

marks.tip: The rules come from a table, not from code or a config file. Changing a rule is one edited row.
`when` is an expression string such as "days > 7". It is run against the facts to see whether it matches.
Basis points: 1000 means 10%. Integer division, so there is no float noise. The rule's name travels with the fee.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE refund_fee_rule (
    id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    position  INT NOT NULL,           -- the first match wins
    name      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,   -- stored on the fee record
    when_expr VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    bp        INT NOT NULL CHECK (bp BETWEEN 0 AND 10000),
    active    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);

INSERT INTO refund_fee_rule (position, name, when_expr, bp) VALUES
    (1, 'defective',    'reason == "defective"',     0),
    (2, 'late-return',  'days > 7',               1000),
    (3, 'changed-mind', 'reason == "changed_mind"', 500);

marks.tip: Rules are tried in this order. Defective items come first, so they pay no fee even after 7 days.
To move the late-return fee from 10% to 15%, update this one row. No code, no deploy.

blocks.body: A fee never changes the original amount. The Refund record states the full amount, and the fee is a separate, linked record.

items: Price: an editable rule is live logic. Let only trusted staff edit it, validate each expression when it is saved, and log who changed what.
When not to: if rules change once a year, a reviewed config file is simpler and safer, but editing it is still a deploy.
Show the user first: "Refund $100, fee $10, you receive $90".
Store which rule applied, by name, on the fee record. It will help in a later dispute.

check.q: Why does moving the fee rules into `services.yaml` still need a deploy, and where can they live so it doesn't?
check.a: `services.yaml` ships with the code, so any change is a deploy. In a database table that staff can edit, a rule change is one updated row.

slides.title: Why is the balance 200? The table won't say
slides.tldr: A CRUD table holds only the current value, so "how did we get here?" has no answer; where that question is the heart of the matter, event sourcing earns its place.

blocks.body: Rachel complains: "I had 500 in my account, so why is it 200 now?" Ryan opens the `account` table and finds a single number: `balance = 200`. Who reduced it, when and why is nowhere in the table. He digs through the logs and tries to guess, because every update overwrote the earlier value.

blocks.caption: Only the current value versus a ledger of every event

columns.title: CRUD table
items: balance = 200
What was it before? Unknown
Why did it drop, and who did it? Unknown
columns.tip: Every UPDATE overwrites the old value with the new one, so no history survives.

columns.title: Event ledger
items: Deposit 500 (day one)
Withdrawal 300 (Saturday, ATM)
Balance = 200, with reasons
columns.tip: Every event stays forever as one line. The current value is the sum of all the lines.

blocks.body: In event sourcing, the events are the truth. The current state is just their sum.

aside.body: In banking, ledgers and insurance, where "how did we get here?" matters legally or commercially, the current value isn't enough. The sequence of events is the real data.

items.meaning: An unchangeable record of something that has already happened, such as MoneyWithdrawn.
Storing the events instead of the state itself, and working the state out from them.

check.q: When you run `UPDATE balance = 200` on a CRUD table, what information is lost forever?
check.a: The previous value (500) and the reason for the change. An ordinary table overwrites the old value on every UPDATE, so history is lost unless you build something extra to keep it.

slides.title: The credit ledger: appending events and replaying them
slides.tldr: The event store only ever grows and never changes; to know the state you replay all events, and when that gets slow you start from a recent running total (a snapshot).

blocks.title: The store's credit ledger
blocks.body: In the ledger where the store owner writes down who owes what, nobody crosses out an old line and writes a new number; new lines are only added at the bottom. To know how much is owed, you add up all the lines. When a page fills up, the owner carries a total forward, so the next page can start from that figure. A mistake isn't scratched out; an opposite line is added.

blocks.caption: A command arrives: replay the earlier events to learn the state, then append a new event

nodes.label: Command
nodes.tip: The request for whatever the user or other code wants to do.

nodes.label: Account
nodes.tip: Owns the business rules. Looks at the earlier events to decide whether a new event is valid.

nodes.label: Event store
nodes.tip: Holds every event in order. Nothing is ever UPDATEd or DELETEd.

edges.label: The command reaches the Account aggregate
The Account gets all its earlier events back (replay)
If the balance is enough, a MoneyWithdrawn event is appended

blocks.body: An account with 10,000 events means reading 10,000 rows on every load. So every 100 events or so you take a **snapshot**: a copy of the state at that moment. Next time you load the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it: fewer than 100, not 10,000.

items.meaning: The thing whose rules are protected together, such as one Account.
A saved copy of an aggregate's state at some moment, used to shorten replay.

aside.body: Events are added, never changed. To fix a mistake, add an opposite event.

check.q: Is the state still correct without a snapshot? Then why take snapshots?
check.a: Yes, replaying all events gives the right state. A snapshot is only for speed: with many events you can start from the latest snapshot instead of replaying everything.

slides.title: The event store and the aggregate in code
slides.tldr: A (aggregate_id, version) primary key on the event_store table blocks concurrent writes; the aggregate rebuilds its state with fromHistory() and keeps new events pending.

blocks.caption: The columns of the event_store table

cells: Which Account the event belongs to
rows.tip: All events of one aggregate are stored under the same id, so they can be read together.

cells: The event's position within that aggregate
rows.tip: (aggregate_id, version) is the primary key. The same version can't be inserted twice, which protects against concurrent writes.

cells: The event's name and structure version
rows.tip: Without schema_v, once the structure changes you can't tell which old event has which structure.
The actual content of the event. occurred_at defaults to now() in the database. This row is never UPDATEd or DELETEd.

marks.tip: Rebuilds state from past events. No rules are enforced here, because the events have already happened.
The rules apply to a new command: you can't withdraw more than the balance.
The new event isn't saved yet; it waits in the pending list.
expectedVersion is the version you saw when you read. Writing starts right after it.
If two people try to write the same version at once, the primary key stops one of them. Optimistic concurrency without a lock.

aside.title: Two withdrawals at once
aside.body: Rachel and her husband each press "withdraw 300" on a balance of 500. Both read version 5, both see 300 is fine, both try to write version 6. Without the primary key both would be saved and the balance would be -100. With it, the second write fails, the command retries on the fresh state (balance 200) and gets InsufficientFunds.

items: Name events in the past tense: `MoneyWithdrawn`, `OrderShipped`. They can't be changed precisely because they have already happened.
On ConcurrentModification, reload and retry the command, because the balance may have changed in the meantime.

check.q: What happens when two people write version 5 to the same Account at once, and why is that good?
check.a: The primary key (aggregate_id, version) stops one of them, who gets a ConcurrentModification. That's good, because one of the two was acting on a balance that has already changed.

slides.title: Snapshots in code: load fast, replay little
slides.tldr: Save the state every 100 events; load() reads the latest snapshot and replays only the events after it. The price: one more table, and a snapshot must be dropped when the rules change.

blocks.body: Without a snapshot, an account with 10,000 events reads 10,000 rows every time it is loaded. With one saved every 100 events, `load()` reads one snapshot row plus fewer than 100 later events. The snapshot is only a shortcut: delete it and the events still give the right answer.

marks.tip: Only events with a version above the snapshot's are read: fewer than 100 rows instead of 10,000.
restore() starts from the saved balance and version, then replays the later events.
Call it after a successful append when the version is a multiple of 100. If it fails, nothing is lost: the events are the truth.

blocks.title: What it costs
items: One more table, and code to keep it fresh.
If you change how `apply()` works, old snapshots are wrong: delete them and let them rebuild from the events.
Under a few hundred events per aggregate, replay is already fast: skip snapshots.
Take snapshots in a background job if you like. A snapshot is only a cache of what the events already say.

check.q: An account has 10,000 events and its latest snapshot is at version 9,900. How many events does `load()` replay?
check.a: 100: only the events with a version above 9,900. The snapshot already holds the state up to 9,900, so replaying those again would be wasted work.

slides.title: A separate table for reading: projections and lag
slides.tldr: In CQRS the write model and the read model are separate; a projector listens to events and updates the read model, so the read model lags slightly (eventual consistency) and the UI must cope.

blocks.body: Replaying the event store every time someone asks "what's the balance?" would be silly. So you listen to the events and maintain a plain `account_balance` table, called a **projection** or read model. You can throw it away and rebuild it from the events. But it updates a moment later, so reading right after a write may show the old value.

blocks.caption: Read right after a write and you may briefly see the old value

actors.label: Rachel
actors.tip: Withdraws money and wants to see the balance straight away.

actors.label: Event store
actors.tip: The source of truth. Writes succeed here immediately.

actors.label: Projector
actors.tip: Listens to events and updates the read model. Runs in the background, so there is a delay.

actors.label: Read model
actors.tip: The account_balance table. Built for reading, so it is fast.

marks.tip: Updates only when this is exactly the next version. A duplicate event doesn't match the version, so nothing changes.
The projector is idempotent: throw the table away, replay every event, and you get the same result.

items.meaning: Keeping the model that handles writes separate from the model that answers reads.
A table built from events to answer one kind of question, such as the balance.
The read side catches up a moment after the write, not at the same instant.

items: Return the `version` in the write response. The Vue app can send `?minVersion=7` to the read API and show "Updating…" until that version arrives, or show its own calculated value meanwhile.
To change a read model, build a new projection and replay all events into it from the start; discard the old one afterwards.

check.q: Rachel withdraws money and immediately sees 500 again. Is that a bug? How would you handle it?
check.a: Not a bug: it is eventual consistency, because the read model updates a moment later. Use the version from the write response to wait until the read model reaches it, or show the value you calculated locally.

slides.title: When it pays off, and the cost of changing old events
slides.tldr: Event sourcing gives you history and audit but costs complexity: projections, replay, snapshots, and upcasting when old events change shape; choose it only when history is the main requirement.

rows.tip: When audit or "how did we get here?" is the core question, this is the difference that matters.

cells: Needs a projection, with some lag
rows.tip: You have to maintain a separate read model and cope with its lag.
The whole team has to learn a new way of thinking, and a wrong choice of tool is hard to debug.

cells: Old events stay; you need an upcaster
rows.tip: You can't change earlier events, so you convert them when reading.

blocks.body: Old events can never be changed, but their structure does. Say `MoneyDeposited` once had only `amount` and now also needs `currency`. The code that converts an old event to the new shape as it is read is called an **upcaster**. These pile up over the years, and they are event sourcing's biggest hidden cost.

marks.tip: It looks at the old schema_v and lifts the event to the new shape step by step. The original event in the database stays untouched.
The aggregate always receives the latest shape, so old versions never leak into its code.

blocks.body: If all you need is the current value, event sourcing is dead weight. It pays off only when history is the main product.

use: Audit and history matter legally or commercially (ledgers, insurance)
You need several kinds of read model, or must see past states
avoid: A small team with no time for this complexity

items: Use it only in the part of the system where history is central (a ledger, say), not everywhere. Keep the rest as plain CRUD.
If you only need an audit trail, an append-only `account_history` table beside a plain CRUD table is far cheaper. Event sourcing is for when the events themselves drive the state.
Keep personal data out of events: store a customer id and keep the details in an ordinary table you can erase, or erasure duties (such as GDPR) become impossible to meet.

check.q: Earlier events can't be changed, so how do old events work with new code after the structure changes?
check.a: At read time an upcaster converts an event with an old schema_v to the latest shape. The original events in the database stay untouched, but the upcaster code piles up year after year.
